name: interface-class
intent: Declare a role as a type that carries only operations and no state, so clients depend on what an object promises to do rather than on the class that happens to supply it.
problem: The type that names a role also carries representation: once clients type their variables to the supplier's class they inherit its fields, its constructor and its implementation choices, and a class that already extends something else or lives in another module cannot join the role at all. Asking two unrelated classes to answer the same protocol - or replacing the supplier with a fake, a decorator or a second implementation - then means editing every client, which is the recurring trigger for a contract that has no separate existence from its first implementation.
context: Applies at the seam between a caller and a replaceable supplier: layered subsystems, ports in a hexagonal architecture, plug-in and extension points, test seams and published libraries. It pays off wherever more than one implementation is expected, wherever implementations arrive from another team or are chosen at run time, or wherever the caller must not depend on the supplier's representation. It assumes the language offers some way to name an operation set (a keyword, a pure abstract class, a protocol or trait) or accepts a documented structural convention where it has none.
benefits: Substitutability: any type that satisfies the contract can be used in the same position, so fakes, decorators, remote stubs and alternative implementations need no client change.
Dependency direction is inverted - clients and implementations both depend on a contract the client side can own, instead of clients depending on a concrete supplier.

Several unrelated classes, including ones that already extend a framework base or live in another module, can satisfy one role, and one class can promise several roles, because the contract contributes neither state nor base-class baggage.
The contract is a testing seam: doubles are written against the declared operations only, so a test never has to construct the real supplier's state.
Contracts stabilise separately from implementations: clients compile against the contract, and languages with default or extension members let the contract grow without breaking every implementor.
The role gets a name, which design discussion, documentation, error messages and tooling can refer to independently of any implementation.
tradeoffs: A published contract is the most expensive surface to evolve: adding an operation breaks every implementor unless the language supplies default members, so contracts tend to freeze early or multiply into versioned variants.

Dispatch indirection: calls through a runtime contract are resolved through a vtable or a boxed value unless the language resolves the contract statically, costing an indirect call and blocking inlining of the implementation.

Only signatures are checked. Invariants, pre/postconditions, thread-safety, nullability and ownership cannot be expressed, so an implementation can satisfy the compiler and still break the role's semantics - the compiler cannot tell.

Adding an operation touches every implementation (the expression problem), so in single-dispatch languages a new operation often needs a second structure such as a visitor, a dispatch table or a default member.

One contract per capability multiplies types: navigation, packaging and API surface all grow, and a contract with a single implementation adds a file, a factory and a name to a call that never varies.

State, identity, equality, serialisation and lifetime policy have no home in a stateless contract, so clients must obtain them out of band - through factories, separate contracts or conventions that the type system does not enforce.

participants.responsibility: Declares the role - the operation signatures, and only where the language allows, constants - and nothing else: no fields, no constructor, no implementation that binds the role to a representation.
A class, struct, record or module that promises to satisfy the contract and supplies the behaviour; it owns whatever state the behaviour needs and is typically reachable only through a factory.
Depends only on the contract: holds contract-typed references, calls the declared operations, and never constructs, downcasts to, or inspects the implementation's representation.
Optional but usual: creates implementations and hands them back as the contract type, keeping construction, configuration and lifetime decisions out of clients.

The language's way of combining contracts - base-interface extension, multiple interface inheritance, trait or protocol composition - so one type can promise several roles without the diamond-state problems of multiple class inheritance.

use_cases: Ports in a layered or hexagonal design: the domain declares what it needs from storage, messaging, clock or payment, and the infrastructure module implements that contract.
Plug-in and extension points: a driver or service-provider contract (JDBC, SAX, logging, storage or payment providers) that third parties implement without touching the host.
Test seams: a fast in-memory fake and the slow real service implement the same contract, so business rules run with no infrastructure at all.
Interchangeable algorithms and wrappers at a call site: pricing rules, serializers or caching decorators that the client selects without naming the concrete type.
Cross-module decoupling: the contract lives where both sides may depend on it, so neither side imports the other and the implementations are compiled and deployed separately.
Roles over existing classes: a class that already inherits from a framework base still promises the contract, which a common state-carrying base class could not express.

Event-driven systems and message brokers: event consumers declare a typed handler contract (message type plus acknowledgement semantics), and the runtime dispatches to any implementation — Kafka consumer, in-process handler, or test fake — without the producer knowing the consumer's representation.

Plugin architectures and service-provider interfaces (Java ServiceLoader, OSGi, Eclipse adapter, VS Code extension host): a host defines a contract that third parties implement, loaded and instantiated at run time, so the host never links against the implementing module.

Middleware and pipeline chains: each stage declares a handler contract (request, response, next-chain reference) and the chain hands an opaque context typed only through the contract — ASP.NET Core, Express/Koa, Django middleware, or gRPC interceptors all follow this pattern.

Interchangeable algorithmic strategies selected at a call site without naming the concrete type: pricing rules, sorting strategies, compression codecs or caching decorators where the policy is injected but the algorithm can be swapped without touching the caller.

Cross-module or cross-team decoupling: the contract lives in a shared package that both sides may depend on, so neither side imports the other's implementation assembly and each team can ship, test and deploy independently.

Cloud SDK client abstractions: the SDK surface is a set of contracts (operation request/response types, configuration, retry policy) so users can swap the wire protocol (REST, gRPC) or inject a test double without recompiling against the cloud's own libraries.

Service interfaces in microservices: each service publishes a typed API contract that other services call, and API gateways or service meshes route to the implementation — consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) validates the contract against both sides.

Java's ServiceLoader: a service interface is loaded with provider implementations discovered at run time, so application code selects providers through the contract instead of naming provider classes.

ASP.NET Core's IMiddleware pipeline: middleware implementations satisfy InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate), and the host composes or replaces stages without clients depending on each middleware class.

Go's implicit interfaces: a consuming package can accept any concrete type with the required method set, so implementations from unrelated packages satisfy the role without a shared base class or registration.
avoid_when: There is exactly one implementation and none is planned: a concrete class, or a function value for a single operation, says the same thing with less indirection.
The contract would carry no operations at all: a marker or an attribute expresses the tag without an empty type and its ceremony.
The interaction is about a data shape rather than behaviour: value objects, records, parameter objects or a schema describe data better than a stateless contract full of getters.

The language checks types structurally and the caller owns the call site (Go, Python typing.Protocol, TypeScript, Ruby duck typing): an explicit nominal contract adds ceremony without adding enforcement unless a second implementation must be named.

The operation is over a pair of types, or a closed set of operations must vary independently of a closed set of variants: multiple dispatch, a visitor or a dispatch table expresses what a single-dispatch contract cannot.
The 'contract' would mirror internal classes that never vary and are never faked: one interface per class doubles every signature for no substitutability payoff.
anti_patterns: Header interface for every class: a one-to-one interface mirroring each class's public methods, so every change is declared twice and nothing can be substituted that was not already the class.
Fat contract: one interface accumulating a subsystem's operations, forcing implementors to stub or throw for members they do not support - the client can no longer tell which members are real.
Constant or state carrier: contracts used to publish constants, mutable static state or getters for the implementation's fields, leaking exactly the representation the pattern removes.
Downcast at the call site: testing the concrete type, constructing the implementation inside the client, or reaching for a class-only member - substitutability claimed but never used.
Contract drift: the implementation grows public operations the contract never declared, or the contract freezes while implementations evolve, so clients start reaching around the contract.
Empty ceremony: a contract whose only implementation is the one the client always uses, adding a file, a factory and a lookup to a call that never varies.

Additive interface change without a default body: adding a required member to a shipped contract breaks every implementation — the correct path is a default/extension body, a new extending contract (DoItPlus extends DoIt), or a new major version; the Eclipse binary-compatibility tables document this as a class of IncompatibleClassChangeError.

Default-method collision: when two interfaces the same class implements both declare a default for the same member, the compiler demands an explicit override — the collision signals a design problem, not merely a naming conflict.

Class does not inherit interface members: in C# before default interface members, calling an interface-declared method on a class instance requires a variable typed as the interface — a class does not expose interface members through its own type, so tests that construct the real class cannot call contract methods without an explicit cast.

Implicit interface drift: once an interface is published, every observable behaviour of every implementation becomes a de-facto contract — Hyrum's Law states that with enough users, all observable behaviours will be depended on, so a silent change in implementation behaviour breaks a consumer who never agreed to that term.

Interface where a wrapper, abstract base class, or capability query is the better alternative: a contract with a single unimplementable operation is a capability query; a shared state-carrying base is an abstract class; a synchronous one-off call is a function value.

Marker interface that cannot be unimplemented: a marker interface (Cloneable, Serializable) forces every implementor to satisfy the marker, and removing it from the type system later is a breaking change — language metadata attributes (Java annotations, .NET attributes, Rust derive macros) express the same intent without the type-level commitment.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the declared operation set, not the supplier's class, is what the client depends on.
Dependency inversion: the contract is owned at the client side, so high-level policy does not depend on low-level detail.
Interface segregation: several role-sized contracts beat one general contract, and no client should be forced to depend on operations it does not use.
Liskov substitution: an implementation is bound by the contract's semantics, not merely by its signatures.
Open/closed principle: new behaviour arrives as a new implementation of the existing contract rather than as an edit to clients - while new operations still touch implementations.
Encapsulation and composition over inheritance: the contract exposes behaviour and hides representation, and lets a type acquire capability by composing an implementation instead of inheriting one.
best_practices: Design the contract from the caller's side, role-sized and behaviour-named; if it seems to need a field, the state belongs in the implementation.
Keep contracts pure: no fields, no constructors, and default bodies only for behaviour derived from the declared operations.
Prefer several small contracts composed (multiple interface inheritance, trait or protocol composition) to one broad contract, and never use a contract as a constants bag.
Hand out implementations as the contract type from a factory or builder, and keep the implementation's constructors non-public so clients cannot bind to them.
Write a contract test - a shared conformance suite every implementation runs - because the compiler checks signatures and never semantics.

Treat a published contract as versioned API: add members only where the language allows non-breaking growth (default or extension members), otherwise publish a new versioned contract and deprecate the old one.
Document what the language cannot check: pre/postconditions, allowed errors, thread-safety, lifetime and nullability, next to the declaration.
Use the language's static contracts (bounds, concepts, type sets) for implementors known at compile time, and keep runtime contracts for implementors that arrive at run time.

Design the contract from the caller's side: a role interface contains only the operations the client actually uses in one interaction, not the full public surface of any existing class — the role is named for the behaviour it enables, not for the implementor.

Ship at least one implementation and at least one API that consumes every published contract — a contract without a validated implementation or a named call site is an unverified abstraction that will drift.

Treat a published contract as a versioned API: use default or extension members for additive changes; otherwise publish a new versioned contract and deprecate the old one rather than breaking existing implementors.

Prefer an abstract base class over an interface when you anticipate adding members and can provide a default implementation — an abstract class allows non-breaking additions where an interface does not.

Wire implementations at a single composition root: it is the only location that names concrete types and calls constructors; libraries and frameworks should expose contracts (and optionally Abstract Factories or Facades) but must never define their own composition root.
Prefer several small contracts composed through multiple inheritance or protocol composition over one broad contract — the Go proverb applies: the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.

Use static contracts (generic bounds, concepts, type sets) for implementors known at compile time; reserve runtime dispatch (trait objects, vtable, boxed values) for implementations that arrive at run time or from separate teams.

Document preconditions, postconditions, allowed errors, thread-safety, lifetime and nullability in prose beside the declaration — no mainstream language enforces these semantically, so they must live where implementors read.

Write a shared conformance test suite that every implementation runs: the compiler checks signatures but not substitutability semantics, and a conformance suite catches drift before it reaches production.
Put the interface in the package that consumes it and return concrete types from providers — this lets implementors add methods without breaking clients that import only the contract.
